notes.meaning: Right after His baptism, the Holy Spirit guided Jesus into the desert to face the devil. The word for tempted also means tested or proved. God permitted this trial so that Jesus could defeat the enemy and sympathize with us when we are tested.

Jesus went without food for forty days and nights, just as Moses and Elijah had done. During this intense time of prayer with the Father, His physical appetite was held back until the fast ended. When hunger set in, His weakened physical condition gave Satan an opening to strike.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Many Catholics observe the forty days of Lent as a way to unite their own self-denial with Christ's forty-day fast in the desert.

notes.meaning: The devil attacked Jesus at His point of physical hunger, urging Him to doubt the Father's love. He dared Jesus to prove His divine Sonship by turning nearby desert stones into loaves of bread. Satan wanted Jesus to act on His own apart from the Father and use His power for selfish relief.

Jesus turned away the devil's bait by quoting the book of Deuteronomy. He explained that bread alone does not keep a person alive, but God's sustaining word and will. Instead of grabbing an unlawful shortcut, Jesus chose to trust His Father to sustain Him.

The devil next led Jesus to Jerusalem, the holy city, and placed Him on a high ledge of the temple. This dizzying spot stood hundreds of feet above the valley floor below. Having failed to make Jesus distrust God, Satan tried to push Him into reckless pride.

Satan challenged Jesus to leap off the ledge, quoting Psalm 91 to claim that angels would catch Him. The devil twisted God's promise of protection into an excuse to stage a reckless public display. He wanted Jesus to presume on God's help without any command from God to take such a risk.

Jesus answered Satan by quoting Deuteronomy once more. God promises to protect His servants in their duties, but jumping into foolish danger simply to see if God will save us is putting Him to an ungodly test. True faith trusts God's care without demanding miracles on demand.

The devil next took Jesus to a very high mountain and displayed all the kingdoms of the world in their splendor. This grand display was a vision designed to stir up earthly ambition. Satan offered Jesus royal power over the nations without the pain of the cross.

Satan offered to hand over his grip on the nations on one condition: Jesus had to bow down and worship him. The devil threw off all disguises and boldly demanded the honor that belongs only to the Creator. It was a wicked bribe asking the Savior to ally Himself with darkness.

Jesus ordered Satan to leave immediately, rebuking him with supreme authority. He quoted Deuteronomy to affirm that religious worship and service belong to God alone. When evil directly attacks God's honor, it must be cast out without hesitation.

Satan was completely defeated and fled from the field of battle. Holy angels then came to serve Jesus, providing food and comforting Him after His long trial. Jesus received from His Father's hands the care He had refused to grab by the devil's shortcuts.

When Jesus learned that John the Baptist had been thrown into prison, He moved north into the region of Galilee. This move was not driven by cowardice, but because John's preparatory work had ended and Jesus' public work was now to expand. When one servant of God is silenced, God raises up another.

Jesus left His boyhood home of Nazareth after the people there rejected His message. He made His new home in Capernaum, a bustling town along the Sea of Galilee in the historic lands of Zebulun and Naphtali. This busy fishing hub gave Him access to large crowds and everyday laborers.

Matthew points out that Jesus chose this region to fulfill ancient Old Testament prophecy. Centuries before, God had promised through the prophet Isaiah that this neglected northern country would receive special grace. Jesus ordered His travels so that God's ancient word would come to pass.

The prophet named the border lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, calling the region Galilee of the Gentiles because many foreign nations lived alongside the Jews there. Due to its distance from Jerusalem and its mixed population, the area was looked down on by religious leaders. Yet God chose this humble border country as the cradle of the gospel.

Sitting in darkness describes living in deep spiritual ignorance, helplessness, and the dread of death. When Jesus arrived and began His ministry, His teaching was like a brilliant sunrise dawning over a hopeless land. The gospel brings understanding and life to people who cannot find their way out of darkness.

Jesus took up the central theme of His public preaching, which matched the message John the Baptist had proclaimed. To repent means to turn away from sin and change one's heart toward God. The kingdom of heaven was near because Christ the King was right in their midst, offering God's gracious rule.

While walking along the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Peter and Andrew, casting a round net into the water. Jesus did not seek His first leaders among the wealthy priests or scholarly scribes in Jerusalem, but among working fishermen. He meets ordinary people in their daily routines and invites them into His work.

Jesus called the two brothers to follow Him and promised to turn them into fishers of men. Instead of catching fish for a living, they would now be trained to bring lost human souls into God's kingdom of safety. Those who serve Christ must first follow Him closely to learn how He loves and teaches.

Peter and Andrew immediately dropped their fishing nets and went after Jesus. Leaving their gear meant walking away from their source of livelihood to follow a penniless teacher. Their ready obedience sets an example of gladly giving up earthly security when the Lord calls.

Walking a little further, Jesus found two more brothers, James and John, sitting in a boat mending nets with their father Zebedee. Jesus called them just as He had called the first pair. Even while they were busy taking care of family tools and chores, they were ready to hear His voice.

James and John instantly left their boat and their father to follow Jesus. While honoring and helping parents is a sacred duty, the call of Christ takes first place above every family bond. The powerful grace in Jesus' word made them willing to leave all behind.

Jesus traveled across Galilee, teaching in local Jewish meeting places called synagogues, preaching the good news of God's rule, and healing every sickness. His miracles proved that His words were true and showed God's tender love for suffering people. By restoring broken bodies, He showed His deeper purpose to heal sick and sinful souls.

Reports of Jesus' power spread far beyond Galilee into the neighboring nation of Syria. People brought Him every kind of suffering person, including the demon-possessed, the paralyzed, and those having seizures, and He cured them all. No sickness or spiritual torment was too severe for His healing word.

Enormous crowds gathered to follow Jesus, coming from Jewish districts like Judea and Jerusalem as well as Gentile areas like the Decapolis. People from different cultures and walks of life were drawn together by His words and works of mercy. This diverse crowd gave an early glimpse of how the gospel would soon welcome people from all nations.
